newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: FEATURE-Offshore fuelling threatens Singapore name.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Offshore fuelling threatens Singapore name.

text.p: An offshore ship refuelling business is blossoming off Singapore, the world's biggest bunkering port, hurting its business and threatening its reputation, industry sources say.
Instead of coming into port, some shipowners refuel their vessels offshore -- beyond the range of Singapore's tough regulations but within its territorial waters.
Industry sources said the off-port-limit (OPL) trade has been growing significantly over the past few years, eating into the port's business and encouraging cheating.
The grey market, although not illegal, is unregulated and some disreputable bunker suppliers provide poor quality fuel or cheat on quantity, they said.
"It's cheap for vessels sailing through Singapore to get bunker outside the port because there are no expensive port fees," said one bunker trader in Singapore.
A shipowner said he could save up to US$2,000 if he took on fuel oil outside the port.
"It's also very time-saving as you don't have to go through all that paperwork," said the trader.
SINGAPORE SALES ARE DROPPING
In 1996, vessels calling at Singapore bought 16.9 million tonnes of bunker fuel, a three percent drop from a year earlier, official figures showed.
But in the grey OPL market, volume almost doubled to three million tonnes over the same period, according to industry estimates.
Some shipowners said they preferred to refuel in-port.
"I am totally againt this (OPL) because it's just not reliable. Port charges are high and it takes time, but I am prepared to pay the money," said one.
Apart from quality and credibility concerns, the shipowner said the OPL trade was causing pollution.
"They are polluting our waters though it is outside the port limits," he said.
"The port authority must do something about it, either to do more checks outside the port or to lower the port fees. They cannot say it's beyond the port's control."
The growing OPL market is adding to the pressure on Singapore's port business, which is facing increasing competition from South Korea and the United Arab Emirates.
South Korea, armed with competitive prices and good fuel quality, is catching up with Singapore as a major bunkering port.

Industry sources estimate South Korea's bunker sales will reach 10 million tonnes in 1997, with a 3.8 percent growth in foreign demand. Of the total, sales to foreign flag vessels are expected to rise to 5.5 million tonnes, they said.

Singapore's bunker sales have dropped by around three percent in each of the past two years and traders said they expected the trend to continue. South Korean bunker sales volume grew by 13 percent in 1996.
SINGAPORE INTENT ON MAINTAINING POSITION
However, the Singapore government has said it will work hard to maintain its position.
"We should, however, not only be satisfied by the high volume of bunker lifted," John Chen, Singapore Minister of State for Communications, told an International Bunkering Conference in early April.
"Singapore strives to distinguish itself as a reliable bunkering port, where cheating is not tolerable," Chen said.

The Maritime and Port Authorities of Singapore (MPA) said it conducts daily patrols within the port as well as areas surrounding the port limit to prevent oil pollution, but the OPL bunkering does not come under the jurisdiction of the MPA.

The MPA urges all vessels to purchase only from those who operate in Singapore port waters "to ensure that their transactions are covered by the Singapore Bunkering Procedure which contain standards that ensure the quantity and quality of bunkers supplied," the MPA said in a written reply to questions.
To encourage in-port bunkering, the MPA is also giving concessionary port dues to vessels taking bunkers in the port if the overall stay in the port does not exceed 96 hours.
"We will continually review our port policy as and when necessary to meet the market requirements," the MPA said.

Bunker fuel oil consumption in the Asia-Pacific region is expected to grow 3.8 percent a year between 1995 and 2000 and 3.4 percent from 2000 to 2005, according to a forecast by Fereidun Fesharaki of Hawaii's East-West Center.
"At the end of the day, it all comes down to the prime concern -- time and money," said a trader with an independent firm in the OPL trade.
"We only deal with old customers and they trust us," he said. "If shipowners can get good quality and cheap stuff and stay away from pirates, why not?"
